M O R E   M A I L ! !

From: Albert Harper, N. IRELAND

Dear friends,

I wish to ask a favour of you. I
wonder if sometime you would
please run an article on monitor
wiring for the Spectrum with
details of which type of monitor
to get. I see from your list you
had details of monitor wiring in
'Drivechat'- OUTLET No. 42,
February 1991.

Could you repeat it sometime as
my TV has packed up and I would
like to get a proper monitor?

I was given another TV but it's
a monster (size) and it's
slightly bonkers too.

I would have sent to Datel for a
+D interface but with my TV
problems I thought it best to
wait. I may be able to get a
secondhand +D and a TV or
monitor with the money.

Your tape/disczine OUTLET is the
tops and I've advised all those
I correspond with to subscribe
to OUTLET. A few have shown
interest in it so I expect you
to get some enquirers seeking
details.

   Your Speccy Friend, (Pest)

          Albert Harper

Brian Cavers to Albert Harper

Well,er.. actually it's intended
that you BUY items on our back
issues list - not simply request
we repeat them! We have to make
a living! However, I am not
completely heartless!You can get
a Philips CM8833 colour monitor
from Microsnips, 25-29 Grange
Road West,Birkenhead,Merseyside,
L41 4BY for `259 + `10 delivery.
Tell them it's for use with your
particular model of Spectrum (it
must be one with a monitor port)
and that you need a cable as
well and say you heard of them
in OUTLET!

Thanks for spreading the word -
much appreciated!
                        - Brian

From: Les Tyler, CHELTENHAM

In reply to James Castle's query
in OUTLET 53 regarding my STD
MASTERFILE datafiles.

The short answer would appear to
be "YES, there is a difference
between the product of the 48K
and +3 versions of MASTERFILE"
although I, personally, was
unaware of it, not having a +3
myself.

I assume the principal differ-
ence is in the file length, etc.
In the 48K version this is
limited to approx 31K of data,
and it is reasonable to assume
that the +3 version provides
file lengths far in excess of
that.

I understand that MASTERFILE is
now marketed by someone other
than Campbell Systems, who, from
my experience over the years
have been most helpful over any
queries, etc. I have raised
concerning their products, and
have gone out of their way to
provide useful POKEs, etc. where
necessary to suit individual
requirements.


I would have thought that, given
their track record, they would
have ensured that the +3 could
access files produced by the
earlier system, and I suggest
that they be contacted if the
suppliers of the program cannot
help.

Not having a +3 I do not know if
I can be of any further assist-
ance in this matter, but if
James, (or anyone else similarly
placed), cares to give me a ring
on 0242 230784, preferably after
7 p.m. most evenings; I will be
glad to do what I can.

Now, a gentle dig at B.G. for
his comment in his reply to
James. "WOT !! ONLY COPY NOW
UNLOADABLE? WHO HASN'T MADE A
BACKUP COPY THEN?" I presume
he is referring to 'MASTERFILE'
+3, in which case I can't help,
but feel, personally he ought to
rectify that situation ASAP!

I have a small problem with
which I hope you can help...

When I first became a subscriber
to OUTLET, I elected to have it
on tape, for various reasons,
among them being that my disc
drives were 40-track and thus
limited to 173K, not always
sufficient to get on the whole
of an OUTLET issue.

By having the tape version I was
able to transfer all, or as much
as I required, to disc, in what-
ever order or form I chose, and
this has proved quite satisfact-
ory for the most part.

A few months ago I acquired an
80-track drive, (it works fine,
Malcolm!), and decided that from
then on I would have the 3.5"
disc version.

Again this has proved fine on
the whole, but one or two snags
have arisen. Using COL80+ with
the earlier set-up I was able to
print out the OUTLET text files
on my serial printer with no
problem, but I am unable to do
so with the newer drive, why, I
know not. (I'm using a Sinclair
128 Plus 1 and print via the
RS232 port on that machine.)

To print out these files, I had
to resort to transferring them
to tape, changing the drives
back to the old ones, and runn-
ing COL80+ from there. A rather
slow process when I had obtained
the newer drive specifically
with speedier access to such
files as these than is available
from tape.

In addition, I am sure it can't
be doing my equipment any good
to keep on changing the drive
connections physically. The
ribbon cables in particular
won't respond too well to
frequent disconnections!


I don't know the manufacturer of
the 3.5" drive, (without undoing
the case) but I suspect it to be
an MGT one. It is a black case
with no visible markings on the
outside.

Are there likely to be any
connections, links, etc. inside
the drive that might need
changing to enable the printer
to be used with these files?

I should add there is no problem
with the normal RS232 printer
usage but just when using COL80+
and the OUTLET text files plus
one other program, where the
trouble is partly known.

As in so many things in the
computer field, (and in others
as well, I might add!) it would
seem that the more sophisticated
bits of equipment one acquires
as time goes by do not always
seem to bring about the expected
improvement in operating
performance and the like!

It looks as if one should never
dispose of any superseded bits
of hard/software unless a
complete clear-out of the whole
system is contemplated.

As sure as eggs is eggs, you're
going to have to revert to some
older bit of kit or software at
some time in the future ! (Which
is, of course, my excuse for all
the bits and pieces I have
acquired over the years and
still jealously guard !!)

Any help on this issue will be
appreciated.

        Cheers !!....Les

Brian Cavers to Les Tyler

You make no reference to any
change of drive interface but
only to a change of drives. This
is weird as I cannot see how the
drive can make any difference to
a print-out! Are you sure you
don't mean you have changed your
interface, e.g., Opus to +D? I'm
sorry if you have discussed your
equipment with me before, Les,
but I deal with so many queries
I can't always remember who has
what! I thought you had Opus but
your record indicates +D. If you
used the +D with 40-track drives
with no print-out problems and
now you have an 80-track drive
with the same +D but get printer
problems then I am baffled!

You say you have been printing
via the Sinclair RS232 port.This
also puzzles me because THERE IS
NO SUCH OPTION in COL-80! Which
option do you use? Let me guess.
Supposing you did have an Opus
and selected the Opus option.
That would use the OPEN # syntax
to open a stream to your printer
by the Opus Discovery Centronics
port. If the Sinclair RS232 port
uses the same syntax (check your
manual if in doubt as I do not
have that machine) then it may
automatically be diverting the
Opus commands and using the
RS232 by sheer chance! However,
the +D or Disciple won't allow
this. Still, in that case you
should have got an error message
"nonsense in BASIC".

You don't mention any error
message (I can't believe you'd
keep such an important piece of
information from me as an error
report when you want me to solve
the error - would you?!?!?) so I
have to assume that when you say
"I am... unable to print out..."
means simply that nothing at all
happens? Does the program "lock
up" waiting for you or does it
continue somehow?

I'd have thought the problem was
that you had just changed to +D
which is not compatible with the
RS232 output, solution: use the
+D Centronics output (assuming
your printer will accept this).
However, you say you CAN print
via the RS232 with everything
but COL-80 even with the +D!!!

Sorry,but this seems unlikely to
me. Can you confirm that again?

This one has me beat but I sus-
pect that you haven't told me
everything!

Is anyone else printing via the
Sinclair RS232 with +D attached
and can they tell me what syntax
is used with the RS232?

Keep in touch, Les but I think
you may end up having to get a
new printer cable or even a new
printer if you want to print
with the +D attached. Hopefully,
it will emerge that I don't know
what I'm talking about.

                        - Brian

From: P. Parnell, LANCASHIRE

Dear Ron,

I placed an ad. in OUTBOARD and
was pleasantly surprised at the
number of replies. In the end Mr
Gordon Roberts supplied the
solution - he even put in a
machine code cat. routine for
me! I see he is starring in
Issue 52.

If you are reading this Gordon
then thanks again! I also got
hold of the DRAGONTORC and so
you can remove my ad from
OUTBOARD. Thank you to all who
rang offering help. What a
friendly bunch you OUTLETeers
are!

I have a number of anomolies you
or your members could perhaps
help me with.

1) I am having problems with
the OUTDEX program. It's not
that it doesn't work properly it
is when using the printer that
the problems start. I have
enclosed a number of printouts
which should show the problems.
I have also enclosed photocopies
of all the relevant pages of my
printer manual.

If you use the OUTDEX program
from scratch it prints in A4
size but with double linespaces.
If you try again, or break in
and run it, then it prints in A3
size double width print again
with double width print!

If you could point out the line
numbers where all the printer
codes are, explaining all the
variables I'd be most grateful.

2) I cannot get the OUTPRINT on
EXTRA No.1 to work. It just
freezes up after it loads. Any
ideas anyone? I seem to recall
someone mentioning this in a
previous letter.

3) The 'BLAST IT' program (Issue
51) doesn't work.Has anyone else
mentioned this as my friend says
his doesn't either. The title
screen is garbled at the
bottom.It DOES work in Issue 52
but the title screen is still
garbled. I havn't tried to print
it out or even know if it does,
so cannot comment on this yet.

4) I am having double line
spacing on the PROCROSS program.
By the way all the double line
spacing is with the dipswitch
set. I get triple if not. Could
you again point out the lines
with the codes as in no.1. I was
also suffering with the TABLOID
option but cured this with a
POKE 64972,0 after GOSUB 9991 in
line 1605 of contents as pointed
out by someone and now have
wonderful hardcopies of the
letters. I reckon this option
has paid for my OUTLETs in saved
paper already!!

5) I am getting double line
spacing (again!) on the print
page/all option. This did not
happen on the older type
OUTLETs.

Could you please point out the
difference or point out a POKE
as in TABLOID problem as this is
driving me potty!

6) The Amstrad DMP4000 also has
a down-loadable font option but
I could not get the program
FONTWIST 2 to work. I will be
honest and point out that I did
not really give it a fair crack
of the whip, nor do I really
understand this facet of the
printer.

7) Could you explain to me the
difference between single,
double and quadruple density
graphics modes and how this
would affect, say printing out
of a screen.

Just one last comment before I
sign off. I much prefer the way
you have set up the letters
page. Sinclair and Sam separate
but still on the disk. I would
not like to see the Sam stuff
axed as although I don't have
one now, you never know, I may
find myself with some cash to
spare and splash out on one!I'll
probably wait a while though
until all is running smoothly.

I feel I must thank you for the
excellent effort you put into
this diskzine. I've been waiting
for something like this for a
long time and only regret not
being in on it from the start.
Perhaps the back issues will
make up for it. Thanks once
again.              PHIL PARNELL

Brian Cavers to Phil Parnell




1.) The OUTDEX problem is weird
as you get a different printout
on two occasions yet running the
same program! OUTDEX uses
ENLARGED/CONDENSED text which
sounds like a contradiction in
terms but gives a slightly
larger text than normal. It does
seem that some printers will not
accept this and so alter line
9889 by removing...


     CHR$ I5;E$;"W";CHR$ I

  ...from the LPRINT statement.

This should give you normal text
but at the left of the page so
you may prefer to replace in the
above LPRINT statement...

    CHR$ 27;CHR$ 108;CHR$ 15;

          ...to give a left-hand
margin and thus centralize the
text.

That still leaves the double
line spacing problem. This
should be cured by changing (in
line 250)...

  LET L$=(CHR$ I0 AND NOT ZX)

             to...

           LET L$=""

Although I don't understand how
you get two linefeeds if you say
your printer is set up not to do
an auto linefeed. Are you sure
about that? What happens when
you LLIST a program because then
the +3 sends its own linefeed at
the end of each line. Do you get
double line spacing then?

2) OUTPRINT prints out perfectly
from my +3 although this is now
really superseded by TABLOID. I
faintly remember a problem with
very large files and it may be
that if you load a giant
OUTLETTERS file it may be over-
writing the code. Try a small
file. If it still fails, give me
more details. Do you mean it
freezes after loading the
program or a textfile?

If it is immediately after the
program loads then you may have
a faulty copy. Return your disc
for replacement if you want to
get it working but as I say, it
is the forerunner of TABLOID and
so redundant really. Are you
sure you have the +3 version?

3) I am aware that part of the
title screen in BLAST IT is
garbled on the +3. This is
purely cosmetic and does not
affect its working and since
it's an ADD-ENDER I am not too
concerned. BLAST IT is an old
program called into service just
for anyone who doesn't have
Tasword 2. I've always had
trouble testing print options on
my +3 because my cable doesn't
reach.

However, I've just realized that
now I have a printer switch I
have extra length! So, I checked
Issue 51's BLAST IT and...
you're right! It seems the BASIC
has corrupted at line 2620 -
weird! Fortunately it is O.K. in
later issues.

4) The only way I can get
PROCROSS to do a double line
feed is if I set my printer dip
switch to auto line feed. Having
done that I can get PROCROSS to
print correctly by doing the
following...

RESET and in +3 BASIC, MERGE
"PROCROSS" (this avoids the loss
of the character set). You will
need to wait half a minute while
it MERGEs.

In each of lines 5200, 5300,
5360 and 5390 there is an
LPRINT CHR$ I0;CHR$ 13. In each
case REMOVE the CHR$ I0; and ADD
a new semi-colon (;) AFTER the
13 thus... CHR$ 13; (there may
be other things in the same
LPRINT but just leave them).

IN ADDITION, remove the single
LPRINT CHR$ I0 at the START of
line 5200. It is important to
remove the word LPRINT totally
here, not just the CHR$ I0.

Now, put a spare disc in the
drive and enter RUN 9972 (+3) to
save a fresh copy (in case you
make a mistake!). Other readers
using microdrive syntax can RUN
9982 while tape users RUN 9983.

I had trouble editing line 5390
in +3 BASIC as the cursor kept
jumping when I pressed DELETE!
This reminds me of a recent
letter (I just forget from who)
pointing out some of the quirks
in +3 BASIC editing and I think
I found one! Take care! The 48K
editor is far better if you type
SPECTRUM and RANDOMIZE USR 23354
after to get back to 128K so you
can use the disc.

5) You say you get double line
spacing when printing from our
text pages but didn't in the
early OUTLETs. The code used in
these text pages of OUTLET has
remained unchanged since we
started in 1987 so this suggests
you have some change in your
hardware.

Perhaps your printer is differ-
ent or your Spectrum? I don't
understand this. Once again, I
can only create this problem by
setting my printer to autofeed.
I have managed to solve it with
a POKE though. MERGE "CONTENTS"
as you did for PROCROSS then
enter...

301 POKE 34797,0

Now,RUN 9970 to erase and resave
it on the same disc. Microdrive
syntax users can RUN 9980 and
tape RUN 9983.

6) Thanks to Bill Coats we now
have FONTWIST.3 in this month's
ADD-ENDERS and this should work
O.K.!

7) In a printer's graphics mode
you are sending vertical strips
of dots which are printed side
by side to make up the image.
Double density graphics mode
just moves the print head half
as far to the right each time so
you end up with twice the number
of dots per inch horizontally.
For instance (magnified!)...

     normal       double density

x x x x x x x x      xxxxxxxx
x             x      x      x
x             x      x      x
x             x      x      x
x             x      x      x
x             x      x      x
x             x      x      x
x x x x x x x x      xxxxxxxx

Quadruple density has four times
the number of dots per inch. As
you can see from the example, a
normal screen printed in double
density would appear squashed
horizontally but be the same
height.

However, just copying a screen
is not the only application of
printer graphics so these higher
densities are more useful with
software that can send higher
resolution graphic data to give
higher quality pictures. There's
not space to go into this here!

Finally, your problem printing
out thad dodgy OUTPUT can be
cured by...
         302 POKE 35290,0

However, that is a temporary fix
for OUTPRINT only as it may mess
up the other headers -I don't
know! I suggest you don't resave
the program.

                       - Brian.

From: Ted Felstead, WIGAN

I've written a program called
'Plots2' as a follow up to plots
in order to cover more advanced
equations. Also, I'm sending a
program called 'Spirals'. I've
included this since I've become
aware, through reading back
issues,that every so often the
issue of copyright appears to
raise its head.

In particular the issue of Grant
Dixon's 'Megadem', (OUTLET 33)
caused me to think a bit as it
seemed that lots of the routines
were based on standard math-
ematical equations with changes
to variables in a random fashion
and then jazzed up a bit to make
them look pretty.

It surely is obvious that the
rules governing mathematics,
physics and chemistry are
universal and belong to no one.

I, in fact, wrote the 'Spirals'
program quite independently
before I saw 'Megadem' and was
intending to include it as part
of 'Plots3'. In fact the spiral
in one form or another has been
used in folklore down the ages,
in particular, the Celts used a
variation of the spiral in their
religion and I believe it has
been used by tribes all over the
world.

Also in Grant's offering were a
3D cube, random rectangles,
random circles, triangles and
ellipses.

I simply refuse to accept that
anyone, other than God himself,
could claim copyright to
material such as this.

I accept that special machine
code routines may have been
written to speed up the
execution but the fact still
remains that this type of
graphic display is a result of
symmetry in nature and can be
achieved easily by anyone.

Does anyone remember the child's
toy called a pantograph?. I had
one, many years ago, and I
achieved some very pretty, and
on the face of it, complex
graphics but so did millions of
others.

A few months ago, when Micronet
was still alive, I sent a very
small BASIC program to Brian
Gaff as a demo of how a simple
loop in a BASIC program could
achieve a quite complex result.

This program was not copied from
any other or extracted from a
listing but came about by
experimentation. The exact same
graphic appeared in 'Megadem'
but did not surprise me in the
least since it was a simple
mathematical equation with a
looped variable.

If it is allowed to claim copy-
right on variations of natural
laws then that spells the death
of all science since it has been

an accepted part or science over
the ages that free exchange of
ideas and information is the
only way that the human race can
step forward. Computers are, as
we all know, only calculating
machines. They are users of
mathematical equations and do
not themselves change the
fundamental laws of mathematics.

          Ted Felstead

Brian Cavers to Ted Felstead

You are absolutely right and I'm
glad you raised this point. I'm
sure that I speak absolutely for
Grant Dixon when I say that he
makes no claim of copyright in
mathematical routines when he
claims copyright for any program
using such routines. I'm sure
Grant would agree with me fully
and that it never occurred to
him to claim copyright in maths
routines. He is only claiming
copyright in the way he uses
them in his program. Even a line
of BASIC might be the same in
another program for example...
LET C = 2*PI*R otherwise how
could anyone calculate even the
circumference of a circle?

Even a sequence of lines may be
the same but the more complex,
the more unlikely two programs
will be EXACTLY the same.I think
I could soon tell if someone had
copied part of someone else's
program (or both had copied that
part from someone else), e.g.,
if all the variables have the
same names and the order is the
same etc.

I've not compared your two prog-
rams but I'm sure you've nothing
to worry about and you can claim
copyright in your own program if
you wish without stopping anyone
else using the same principles
of mathematics.

     - Pythagoras(Oi,YOU!)Cavers

From: Robert Little, SURREY

Is there any'Advice-Line'service
that accompanies the magazine?

Which assembler/debugger would
you especially recommend? I'd
prefer one that is reasonably
user-friendly but also quite
powerful.

I would have printed this using
a word-processor but I thought
you might prefer it under the
'messages' heading on the top of
the order form but as you can
see the writing gets a little
cramped towards the end so as
not to go over the perforation!

            R. Little


Brian Cavers to R. Little

If, by "advice-line" you mean a
telephone service then no,we put
all our queries in these pages
of OUTLET so they can be shared
with other users. This has many
advantages: 1. All other readers
with the same problem get the
answer too! 2. Other readers
frequently ADD to the info given
correct it when wrong or send
complete solutions when we don't
know (this way you are drawing
on the skill and experience of
hundreds and hundreds of other
users -not just us). 3. Others
get the relief of knowing that
others are in the same boat and
it's not just their stupidity!
4. It adds to everyone's know-
ledge and is interesting anyway!

Here's a good example because,
regarding your inquiry after a
"powerful" assembler I seem to
remember one praised in these
pages called "ASTRA"or something
like that. Hopefully, one of our
readers will send some info on
this because I cannot trace a
supplier.

I started with PICTURESQUE (now
called CODE MACHINE) and still
use its debugger which is very
good. However, I don't believe
it is still on sale commercially
so you may have to scour the
small ads in magazines like
MICROMART or hunt around some of
the ALL-FORMAT FAIRS unless any-
one knows from where it may be
bought.

As for assemblers, we have two
good ones at very low cost!...

JACKSOFT (OUTLET 12 or EXTRA 1)

and...

DR. KODE (OUTLET 39)

Both of these have full-screen
editors and are excellent value
since they come for the price of
OUTLET and you get all the other
goodies as well!They do not have
debuggers. We do have a simple
dis-assembler in OUTLET 13 named
OUTSTART. All of these are more
than adequate for my own needs.
I am less concerned about"power"
and more interested in how easy
to use a product is - and these
all are!

The "message" section on our
order form is really intended
for messages to readers that are
generated by our database but I
suppose they can be used for
brief messages about an order or
bad disc returned etc. For any
letters with queries about your
computer, printer, programs or
whatever, I'd much prefer you to
send a text file as we have to
pay for a typist to type them in
and there is time wasted as well
as greater chance of error! All
discs, tapes etc. are returned
with an acknowledgement. However
we hate rules here so we accept
letters in any form really. Just
spare a thought for us though!
(No, not one of THEM sort of
thoughts).
                        - Brian

Brian Cavers to George Wells.

Oh Crikey - it's that old git
again.

To print the clip art from a +3,

1.) The OUTDEX problem is weird as you get a different printout on two occasions yet running the same program! OUTDEX uses ENLARGED/CONDENSED text which sounds like a contradiction in terms but gives a slightly larger text than normal. CHR$ I5;E$;"W";CHR$ I

In each of lines 5200, 5300, 5360 and 5390 there is an LPRINT CHR$ I0;CHR$ 13. In each case REMOVE the CHR$ I0; and ADD a new semi-colon (;) AFTER the 13 thus... CHR$ 13; (there may be other things in the same LPRINT but just leave them).

IN ADDITION, remove the single LPRINT CHR$ I0 at the START of line 5200. It is important to remove the word LPRINT totally here, not just the CHR$ I0.

Now, put a spare disc in the drive and enter RUN 9972 (+3) to save a fresh copy (in case you make a mistake!). Other readers using microdrive syntax can RUN 9982 while tape users RUN 9983.

I had trouble editing line 5390 in +3 BASIC as the cursor kept jumping when I pressed DELETE! This reminds me of a recent letter (I just forget from who) pointing out some of the quirks in +3 BASIC editing and I think I found one! Take care! The 48K editor is far better if you type SPECTRUM and RANDOMIZE USR 23354 after to get back to 128K so you can use the disc.

5) You say you get double line spacing when printing from our text pages but didn't in the early OUTLETs. The code used in these text pages of OUTLET has remained unchanged since we started in 1987 so this suggests you have some change in your hardware.

Perhaps your printer is differ- ent or your Spectrum? I don't understand this. Once again, I can only create this problem by setting my printer to autofeed. I have managed to solve it with a POKE though. MERGE "CONTENTS" as you did for PROCROSS then enter...

301 POKE 34797,0

Now,RUN 9970 to erase and resave it on the same disc. Microdrive syntax users can RUN 9980 and tape RUN 9983.

6) Thanks to Bill Coats we now have FONTWIST.3 in this month's ADD-ENDERS and this should work O.K.!

7) In a printer's graphics mode you are sending vertical strips of dots which are printed side by side to make up the image. Double density graphics mode just moves the print head half as far to the right each time so you end up with twice the number of dots per inch horizontally. For instance (magnified!)...

normal       double density


x x x x x x x x      xxxxxxxx

Quadruple density has four times the number of dots per inch. As you can see from the example, a normal screen printed in double density would appear squashed horizontally but be the same height.

However, just copying a screen is not the only application of printer graphics so these higher densities are more useful with software that can send higher resolution graphic data to give higher quality pictures. There's not space to go into this here!

From: Ted Felstead, WIGAN

I've written a program called 'Plots2' as a follow up to plots in order to cover more advanced equations. Also, I'm sending a program called 'Spirals'. I've included this since I've become aware, through reading back issues,that every so often the issue of copyright appears to raise its head.

In particular the issue of Grant Dixon's 'Megadem', (OUTLET 33) caused me to think a bit as it seemed that lots of the routines were based on standard math- ematical equations with changes to variables in a random fashion and then jazzed up a bit to make them look pretty.

It surely is obvious that the rules governing mathematics, physics and chemistry are universal and belong to no one.

I, in fact, wrote the 'Spirals' program quite independently before I saw 'Megadem' and was intending to include it as part of 'Plots3'. In fact the spiral in one form or another has been used in folklore down the ages, in particular, the Celts used a variation of the spiral in their religion and I believe it has been used by tribes all over the world.

Also in Grant's offering were a 3D cube, random rectangles, random circles, triangles and ellipses.

I simply refuse to accept that anyone, other than God himself, could claim copyright to material such as this.

I accept that special machine code routines may have been written to speed up the execution but the fact still remains that this type of graphic display is a result of symmetry in nature and can be achieved easily by anyone.

Does anyone remember the child's toy called a pantograph?. I had one, many years ago, and I achieved some very pretty, and on the face of it, complex graphics but so did millions of others.

A few months ago, when Micronet was still alive, I sent a very small BASIC program to Brian Gaff as a demo of how a simple loop in a BASIC program could achieve a quite complex result.

This program was not copied from any other or extracted from a listing but came about by experimentation. The exact same graphic appeared in 'Megadem' but did not surprise me in the least since it was a simple mathematical equation with a looped variable.

If it is allowed to claim copy- right on variations of natural laws then that spells the death of all science since it has been

an accepted part or science over the ages that free exchange of ideas and information is the only way that the human race can step forward. Computers are, as we all know, only calculating machines. They are users of mathematical equations and do not themselves change the fundamental laws of mathematics.

Ted Felstead

Even a sequence of lines may be the same but the more complex, the more unlikely two programs will be EXACTLY the same.I think I could soon tell if someone had copied part of someone else's program (or both had copied that part from someone else), e.g., if all the variables have the same names and the order is the same etc.

I've not compared your two prog- rams but I'm sure you've nothing to worry about and you can claim copyright in your own program if you wish without stopping anyone else using the same principles of mathematics.

- Pythagoras(Oi,YOU!)Cavers

```text

```

Графический режим с двойной плотностью просто сдвигает печатающую головку каждый раз в два раза меньше по горизонтали, в результате чего вы получаете вдвое больше точек на дюйм по горизонтали. Например (в увеличении!):

```text
     обычная      двойная плотность

x x x x x x x x      xxxxxxxx
x             x      x      x
x             x      x      x
x             x      x      x
x             x      x      x
x             x      x      x
x             x      x      x
x x x x x x x x      xxxxxxxx
```

Четверная плотность имеет в четыре раза больше точек на дюйм. Как вы можете видеть из примера, нормальный экран, напечатанный в режиме двойной плотности, будет выглядеть сплюснутым по горизонтали, но сохранит прежнюю высоту.

Тем не менее, простое копирование экрана — не единственное применение принтерной графики, поэтому такие более высокие плотности полезнее для программного обеспечения, которое может передавать графические данные с более высоким разрешением для получения снимков более высокого качества. Здесь нет места, чтобы вдаваться в подробности!

```text
10 LOAD "FILENAME" SCREEN$

20 COPY
```

Вместо обычной `COPY` можно ввести `COPY EXP`, чтобы получить более качественный, но медленный отпечаток, а также можно использовать `COPY EXP INVERSE`, чтобы инвертировать изображение.
